 Moon phase today: What the Moon will look like on October 20, 2026
 We're moving towards the Full Moon. 
  By 
 Lois Mackenzie 
 Lois Mackenzie 
 Lois Mackenzie is a freelance reporter at Mashable. Over the years she has written for many publications, covering everything from the local news to the best pair of running shoes. You can find bylines in publications including Fit&Well, Metro, and Coach magazine, usually covering deals on everything from earbuds to TVs, or guides on how to beat your half marathon time.

 The Moon is more than half illuminated, which means we're getting closer to the Full Moon. Each night the Moon will appear bigger in the sky, with lots of opportunity to spot some features on its surface.
 What is today's Moon phase?
 As of Tuesday, Oct. 20, NASA's Daily Moon Guide tracker tells us the Moon is in the Waxing Gibbous phase, with 65% of its surface visible. 
 Tonight, you should be able to spot the Mare Crisium, the Tycho Crater, and Mare Fecunditatis without any visual aids. If you have binoculars you'll also see the Endymion Crater, the Alphonsus Crater, and the Appenine Mountains. Plus, if you have a telescope, you'll also see the Apollo 15 and 16 landing spots, plus the Rima Hyginus.

 When is the next Full Moon?
 The next Full Moon will take place on October 25 or 26, depending on your timezone.
 What are Moon phases?
 The Moon takes around 29.5 days to travel around Earth, and its appearance changes throughout the month. As it moves around our planet, we see different amounts of its sunlit side, from a slim crescent to the quarter phases and eventually a Full Moon. It then begins the cycle again. As NASA explains, these phases are caused by the Moon's changing position relative to Earth and the Sun.
 The eight phases are:

 New Moon - The Moon is between Earth and the sun, so the side we see is dark (in other words, it's invisible to the eye).
 Waxing Crescent - A small sliver of light appears on the right side (Northern Hemisphere).
 First Quarter - Half of the Moon is lit on the right side. It looks like a half-Moon.
 Waxing Gibbous - More than half is lit up, but it's not quite full yet.
 Full Moon - The whole face of the Moon is illuminated and fully visible.
 Waning Gibbous - The Moon starts losing light on the right side. (Northern Hemisphere)
 Third Quarter (or Last Quarter) - Another half-Moon, but now the left side is lit.
 Waning Crescent - A thin sliver of light remains on the left side before going dark again.
